519.title: Depart from me (Luke 5:1–11)
519.hook: after the huge catch, Peter falls down: I'm a sinful man; Jesus says fear not
519.howItsDone: Christians read the great catch of fish as the call of the first disciples, and some churches use "launch out into the deep" to encourage people to begin something new in faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a doorway at sunset, and hands laid on every one of them. Who got your full attention, phone down, to the end of their sentences? Day five hundred nineteen.

Simon has been up all night, and he has nothing to show for it: sore arms, cold hands, empty nets. He and his partners are on the shore now, washing their nets, which is the last chore before sleep. And a crowd is pressing in on a teacher by the water, so close he steps into Simon's boat and asks him to push off a little. Simon does. Jesus sits and teaches from the boat. Fine. Then, when he's finished, he turns to the tired fisherman and says something no fisherman wants to hear at the end of a bad night: let's go out again.
screen: `A NIGHT SHIFT WITH NOTHING TO SHOW.`

segments.voice: "Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught." Listen to Simon's answer in the King James words, tired and honest at once: "Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net." We have toiled. Nevertheless. That word holds both his exhaustion and his trust. And the nets fill so full they start to tear. They wave to their partners in the other boat, and both boats fill until they begin to sink. Now here's the surprise. You'd expect Simon to celebrate a catch like that. Instead: "he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord." Go away from me. In Luke's telling, Simon looks at what has just happened, then at himself, and he wants distance. People still do something like it: when kindness comes unexpectedly, some of us deflect, or joke, or say you shouldn't have. Jesus doesn't argue with Simon about whether he's a sinner. He doesn't go away either. He says: "Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men." Luke's Greek word for catch here is zogreo, which lexicons give as to take alive. Not catching fish for the market, but catching to keep alive, the way you pull someone out of the water. And Luke ends: "they forsook all, and followed him." Two boats full of fish, left on the beach.
screen: `DEPART FROM ME; I AM A SINFUL MAN.`
then, large: `FEAR NOT; FROM HENCEFORTH THOU SHALT CATCH MEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't hide from goodness. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time someone was kind to you and you pushed it away. A compliment you argued with. A gift you said was too much. Help you refused because you didn't want to owe anyone. Notice the small voice that says depart from me, I don't deserve this. Don't fight it; just see it. Then imagine that same kindness coming toward you again, and this time you don't step back. You let it land. Breathe in, and receive it. Breathe out, and let the old embarrassment go. If you pray, you can hear Jesus' answer to Simon as if it were spoken to you: fear not. If you don't, simply let the kindness stay. The bell holds the time.
Zogreo, Luke's Greek word for catching alive: Simon's cry after the great catch, overwhelmed by goodness, and the answer he gets instead, fear not.
Your line: fear not. The next time someone is good to you today, don't deflect. Say thank you, and let it land. Day five hundred nineteen.

520.title: Take up your bed (Luke 5:12–26)
520.hook: a leper touched, and a man let through a roof by friends
520.carry: we have seen strange things today
520.howItsDone: Many Christians point to the friends on the roof when they pray for others or help someone who can't help themselves, sometimes called carrying someone in prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a tired fisherman, a breaking net, and depart from me. Your line was fear not. When kindness came your way, did you let it land? Day five hundred twenty.

Two people today who can't get close to Jesus on their own. The first is a man "full of leprosy," as Luke puts it. In the Bible, leprosy covers a range of skin diseases, and it meant living apart, kept at a distance from family and worship. He falls on his face and says: "Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean." Not can you. If you want to. And Luke says Jesus "put forth his hand, and touched him." Before the healing, the touch. Maybe the first touch the man had felt in years. The second person is lying on a mat in a house so crowded no one can get in the door.

Jesus is teaching inside a house, and the room is packed with teachers of the law from all over, from Galilee, Judea, even Jerusalem. Some men arrive carrying their friend, who is paralyzed, on a bed. They can't get through the crowd. So they climb onto the roof. In the King James words: they "let him down through the tiling with his couch into the midst before Jesus." Picture it: dust falling, tiles lifted, a mat swaying down on ropes into the middle of a lecture. Then this line: "And when he saw their faith, he said unto him, Man, thy sins are forgiven thee." Their faith. The friends'. The man on the mat may not have said a word. His friends' faith carried him through the roof. The teachers in the room ask a serious question, and a fair one from their scriptures: "Who can forgive sins, but God alone?" Jesus answers by doing the visible thing so they'll believe the invisible one: "Arise, and take up thy couch, and go into thine house." And the man stands, picks up the bed that carried him, and walks home praising God. Then Luke's best line, the whole room in one sentence: "We have seen strange things to day." The Greek word is paradoxa, things contrary to what anyone expected. It's where English gets paradox. A man who couldn't walk carrying his own bed. A roof with a hole in it. Christians see in this scene who Jesus is. Anyone can see in it what good friends are.
screen: then, large: `WE HAVE SEEN STRANGE THINGS TO DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help someone get where they need to be. Settle, and breathe. Picture the friends on the roof, sweating, lifting tiles, lowering the ropes slowly. Now think of someone in your life who can't get where they need to be on their own right now. Someone who needs a ride to an appointment. Someone who needs an introduction, a reference, a hand with a form. Someone who needs carrying for a while, because they're too tired or too sad to walk. Let one person come to mind. Then think of the roof: is there a creative way around the crowd? A call, an errand, a door you can open. If you pray, you can carry that person to God in your mind. If you don't, simply carry them in your thoughts. The bell holds the time.
Paradoxa, Luke's Greek word for strange things, beyond all expecting: a paralyzed man's friends lower him through a roof, and he rises, takes up his own bed, and walks home praising God.
Your line: we have seen strange things today. Do the one thing that helps your person get where they need to go, and if it takes a little ingenuity, so much the better. Day five hundred twenty.

521.title: The new wine (Luke 5:27–39)
521.hook: Levi's big feast, and no one after drinking old wine wants new
521.howItsDone: Christians remember Levi as Matthew, the tax collector who became an apostle, and many churches read the call of Levi as a picture of welcome at the table.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hole in a roof and a man who took up his bed. Your line was we have seen strange things today. Did you help someone get where they needed to go? Day five hundred twenty-one.

A tax booth on a road near the lake. Levi sits behind it, collecting customs on goods passing through. It's steady money, and it does not make him popular. Earlier in Luke, John the Baptist tells tax collectors to collect no more than they're owed, which says something about their reputation. Jesus walks up and says two words: "Follow me." And Luke says, "he left all, rose up, and followed him." No negotiation. No two weeks' notice. Then Levi does what people do when their life changes overnight. He throws a party. A big one, in his own house. And he invites everyone he knows, which, for a tax collector, means a lot of other tax collectors.

Some Pharisees and their scribes watch the feast and ask the disciples: "Why do ye eat and drink with publicans and sinners?" For them, who you ate with mattered; a shared table was a sign of belonging, and they took holiness seriously. Jesus answers: "They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." Then they ask about fasting: John's disciples fast, yours eat and drink. And Jesus answers with pictures from the kitchen. Nobody tears a patch from a new coat to fix an old one. Nobody pours new wine into old wineskins: "else the new wine will burst the bottles, and be spilled." Bottles here are wineskins, leather bags. New wine is still fermenting, still giving off gas and stretching. An old skin, already stretched and stiff, can't give anymore, and it splits. "But new wine must be put into new bottles; and both are preserved." Something new needs room to grow. And then a last line, and it's almost a joke: "No man also having drunk old wine straightway desireth new: for he saith, The old is better." Jesus knows people. We like what we know. New wine tastes rough at first. Readers have heard this many ways: some as gentle patience with people slow to change, others as a wry smile at how hard change is. Either way, it's honest. Levi changed overnight. Others take longer. The text seems to make room for both.
screen: then, large: `NEW WINE MUST BE PUT INTO NEW BOTTLES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try a new habit gently. Settle, and breathe. Think of something new you've wanted to start: a few minutes of quiet in the morning, a walk, reading, calling someone more often, going to bed earlier. If part of you says the old way is fine, notice it. That's not a villain; it's just old wine talking. Now, instead of a big plan, picture the smallest new skin you could make room for. One minute instead of thirty. One evening a week, not every night. Something that can stretch as it grows. Imagine doing it today, gently, without forcing it. If you pray, you can ask for patience with your own pace. If you don't, simply let the small new thing feel welcome. The bell holds the time.
The new wine. Jesus' picture of something alive and growing that needs a new container, and his honest line that people who like the old rarely want the new right away.
Your line: new wine takes time. Do your tiny new thing today, and if part of you still prefers the old, smile at it and do the new thing anyway. Day five hundred twenty-one.

522.title: All night on the mountain (Luke 6:1–16)
522.hook: before choosing the twelve, he prays all night
522.howItsDone: Christians often pray before major decisions, and some keep a night or a day of prayer before an important choice, remembering Jesus' night on the mountain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Levi's feast and the new wine. Your line was new wine takes time. Did your tiny new habit get its first day? Day five hundred twenty-two.

How do you make a decision that will shape the rest of your life? A job, a move, a marriage, who to trust. Some people make lists. Some ask friends. Some lie awake at three in the morning, scrolling. Luke shows how Jesus made one such choice: picking the small group who would carry his work after him. The chapter starts with arguments: his disciples picking grain on the sabbath, a man with a withered hand healed in a synagogue, and tempers rising over what the sabbath is for. Jesus asks: is it lawful on the sabbath to do good, or to do evil? And then, before the choice, he leaves the noise behind and climbs.
screen: `HOW DO YOU MAKE A BIG CHOICE?`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "And it came to pass in those days, that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God." All night. Not a quick word before bed. Hours in the dark, on a hillside, alone. Luke keeps showing Jesus at prayer. He prays at his baptism. He slips away to lonely places to pray. He'll pray before Peter names him the Christ, and on another mountain before his face changes. In Luke, prayer keeps turning up at the turning points. Then: "And when it was day, he called unto him his disciples: and of them he chose twelve, whom also he named apostles." The Greek word is apostolos, someone sent out, an envoy. Twelve, and many readers hear an echo of the twelve tribes of Israel. And Luke gives the names: Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother; James and John; Philip and Bartholomew; Matthew and Thomas; James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon called the Zealot; Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot. And at the end of the list, a short phrase: Judas Iscariot, "which also was the traitor." A whole night of prayer, and the list still includes the man who will betray him. Luke doesn't explain that, and doesn't try. What the text does show is this: praying first didn't guarantee an easy outcome. In Luke's telling, the choice was made in prayer, eyes open, at dawn.
screen: `JUDAS TOO, AFTER A NIGHT OF PRAYER.`
then, large: `HE CONTINUED ALL NIGHT IN PRAYER TO GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a big choice before you make it. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a decision in front of you, big or medium. Don't solve it. Don't run the pros and cons again. Just hold it, the way you'd hold a stone in your hand, feeling its weight. Notice what you're afraid of. Notice what you're hoping for. Let the quiet do some of the work that the lists can't. If you pray, you can bring the choice to God without asking for an answer yet. If you don't, simply hold it in silence and see what rises. The bell holds the time.
Apostolos, Greek for one who is sent out, an envoy: the name Jesus gives the twelve, chosen at dawn after he prayed through the night alone on a hillside.
Your line: pray first. Before the next real decision you make today, stop for one minute of quiet first. Then choose. Day five hundred twenty-two.

523.title: The plain (Luke 6:17–26)
523.hook: Luke's beatitudes: blessed are you poor, and woe to you who are rich
523.tomorrow: give, and it will be given
523.howItsDone: Christians often read Luke's Sermon on the Plain alongside Matthew's Sermon on the Mount, and some churches and charities draw on Luke 6:20–21 in their work with the poor and hungry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a whole night of prayer on the mountain before the twelve were chosen. Your line was pray first. Before your last real decision, did you stop for a minute of quiet? Day five hundred twenty-three.

In Matthew, the Beatitudes come from a mountain: Jesus goes up, sits down, and teaches. Luke tells it differently, and the difference starts with the ground. After the night of prayer, Jesus comes down with the twelve and "stood in the plain." The Greek means a level place. Not above the crowd. On the same ground as everyone. And the crowd is huge and mixed, from Judea and Jerusalem, and from the coast of Tyre and Sidon, outside Israel. People pushing forward to touch him, because, as Luke says, power was coming out of him and healing them all. Then he looks at his disciples, and starts to speak.

In the King James words: "Blessed be ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are ye that hunger now: for ye shall be filled. Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh." Notice three things. First, Luke's version says you. Blessed are you poor, not blessed are the poor in general. He's talking to the people in front of him, hungry ones, crying ones. Second, the word now. Hungry now, weeping now. This isn't the final word on their lives. Third, Matthew has blessed are the poor in spirit, and Luke has simply ye poor. Christians read the two side by side. Some stress actual poverty, as in the Catholic teaching sometimes called the preferential option for the poor; others stress the humble heart that knows it needs God. Then Luke does something Matthew doesn't. He turns the blessings over, and on the other side are woes. "But woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your consolation. Woe unto you that are full! for ye shall hunger. Woe unto you that laugh now! for ye shall mourn and weep." Four blessings, four woes, like a coin with two faces. Woe in Greek is ouai, a cry rather than a curse; some readers hear it as alas, a warning said with sorrow. The blessed in Luke aren't the ones who seem to be winning. They're the hungry and the grieving, the ones on level ground. And the comfortable are warned, sadly, that comfort can become all the reward there is.
screen: then, large: `BLESSED BE YE POOR: FOR YOURS IS THE KINGDOM OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at who is blessed here. Settle, and breathe. Picture the level place, the crowd pressing in. Now picture your own neighborhood, your own commute. Who is hungry now? Who is weeping now? Who is the person people step around? Let a few faces come: the man outside the grocery store, the coworker who's been quiet since the funeral, the neighbor who's always short at the end of the month. In Luke, these are the ones Jesus calls blessed. Hold each face for a breath. Then ask, gently, which side of the coin you're on today, and what it would mean to stand on level ground with them. If you pray, you can hold them before God. If you don't, simply see them. The bell holds the time.
The plain. In Luke, Jesus teaches the Beatitudes on a level place, speaking to the poor, the hungry and the weeping as you, and adding four woes.
Your line: blessed are you poor. Today, look properly at one person most people overlook, learn their name if you can, and treat them as someone Jesus called blessed. Day five hundred twenty-three.

524.title: Give, and it will be given (Luke 6:27–38)
524.hook: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over
524.howItsDone: Christians often read Luke 6:38 as a call to generous giving, alongside the Golden Rule in Luke 6:31.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plain, four blessings and four woes. Your line was blessed are you poor. Whose name did you learn, and how did they look at you? Day five hundred twenty-four.

At a grain market, you hold out your measure, a basket or a jar, and the seller fills it. A stingy seller fills it loosely, full of air pockets, and levels it off flat. A generous one does something else. He pours the grain in, then presses it down with his hand. Shakes the container so the grain settles. Pours in more. Presses again. Keeps going until it's heaped up and spilling over the sides, and you have to hold out the fold of your robe to catch the rest. That's the picture Jesus ends this teaching with. But first, he says some very hard things.

Still on the level place, Jesus says, in the King James words: "Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you, Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you." Turn the other cheek. Give to everyone who asks. Lend, hoping for nothing back. And the line now called the Golden Rule: "as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise." Then the center of it all: "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful." Mercy is the measure. And then the picture from the market: "Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom." Bosom here isn't your chest. The Greek word, kolpos, can mean the lap or the fold of a robe, which could hold grain like a pouch. So the image is a lap overflowing. And then the hinge: "For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again." Mete means to measure out. Whatever size of basket you use on others is the basket that comes back to you. This isn't a get-rich promise. A few lines earlier, Jesus has told people to lend, hoping for nothing again. In its place, the measure is about mercy: judge not, condemn not, forgive, give, and the same measure comes back. The basket you hold out to others is the basket you're handed. Running over.
screen: then, large: `GIVE, AND IT SHALL BE GIVEN UNTO YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give with a heaped measure. Settle, and breathe. Picture your hands as the seller's hands at the market, holding a basket of grain. Now think of someone you could give to today. It might be money, but it might be time, praise, patience, attention, a long phone call. Notice your first instinct about how much: level it off, just enough. Now picture pressing it down. Shaking it together. Adding a bit more. What would the heaped version look like? A longer visit. A bigger tip. A real compliment instead of a quick one. Decide on the generous version. If you pray, you can ask for open hands. If you don't, simply picture the basket overflowing. The bell holds the time.
Give. Jesus' teaching on the plain: be merciful, give without counting, and what you give comes back pressed down, shaken together and running over.
Your line: running over. Give the heaped version of whatever you planned to give today, and watch what spills back. Day five hundred twenty-four.

525.title: Blind guides (Luke 6:39–49)
525.hook: a good person out of the good treasure of the heart brings good
525.carry: out of the heart the mouth speaks
525.howItsDone: Christians often quote the mote and the beam as a check before judging others, and the house built on the rock is a familiar Sunday school song and sermon picture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the grain market and the heaped measure. Your line was running over. What did you give the heaped version of, and did anything spill back? Day five hundred twenty-five.

"Can the blind lead the blind? shall they not both fall into the ditch?" Jesus says it almost like a riddle, the kind of saying you'd hear at a village well. It's the last stretch of the sermon on the plain, and the tone changes. After the big things, love your enemies, give with a heaped measure, he turns to something closer to home: the people who try to guide others. Parents. Teachers. Bosses. Friends who give advice. Anyone who's ever said here's what you should do. Which is everyone. And he offers a handful of quick pictures, one after another, like snapshots from a working village: a ditch, a speck of dust, a fig tree, a storehouse, a house in a flood.
screen: `A DITCH, A SPECK, A TREE, A HOUSE.`

segments.voice: First, the speck: "And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but perceivest not the beam that is in thine own eye?" A mote is a speck of dust. A beam is a wooden roof beam. The picture is meant to be funny: a man with a plank sticking out of his face, squinting at his friend's eyelash. Fix your own sight first, then you can help. Second, the tree. Good trees bear good fruit. "For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes." You don't judge a tree by its label; you judge it by what grows on it. Third, the heart, and today's center: "A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil: for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh." Treasure here is thesauros, a storehouse, the place where you keep things. Whatever you've been storing up comes out when you open your mouth, especially when you're tired or surprised. Words are the fruit; the heart is the tree. And finally the house. Someone who hears and does is like a man who "digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock." The flood comes, and the house stands. Someone who hears and doesn't do built on bare earth, and the flood takes it. So the blind guide isn't someone without sight in their eyes. It's someone who hasn't looked inward, whose storehouse is empty, who talks without doing.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak from the good in you. Settle, and breathe. Picture your heart as a storehouse, shelves and barrels. What have you been storing this week? Worry, resentment, gratitude, a kind thing someone said, a grudge, a song. Look honestly. Then think of the words that came out of you lately, especially the quick ones. Do you recognize where they came from? Now find something good on those shelves: a memory of kindness, a person you admire, something that made you laugh. Hold it for a few breaths. That's the treasure you want your words to come from today. If you pray, you can ask for a good storehouse. If you don't, simply rest with the good thing you found. The bell holds the time.
Blind guides. Jesus' warning about guiding others without looking inward first, and his picture of words coming out of the storehouse of the heart.

Your line: out of the heart the mouth speaks. Before you give advice today, check for a beam in your own eye. And look back at the week: a breaking net, a hole in a roof, new wine, a night of prayer, the plain, a heaped measure, a storehouse. Day five hundred twenty-five, and another week on the path.
